title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals
short: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals
lead: Every substitution so far, polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates included, is a transformation of one region onto another. This section studies transformations of the plane and of space, measures how they stretch small rectangles by the Jacobian, and changes the variables of double and triple integrals.
objectives: Determine the image of a region under a given transformation of variables.
Compute the Jacobian of a given transformation.
Evaluate a double integral using a change of variables.
Evaluate a triple integral using a change of variables.
summary_html:
• A transformation $T$ is a function that transforms a region $\kG$ in one plane (space) into a region $\kR$ in another plane (space) by a change of variables.
  • A transformation $\kT:\kG\to \kR$ defined as $\kT(u,v)=(x,y)$ $(\text{or}\;\kT(u,v,w)=(x,y,z))$ is said to be a one-to-one transformation if no two points map to the same image point.
  • If $\kf$ is continuous on $\kR,$ then $\iint\limits_{\kR}\kf(x,y) dA=\iint\limits_{\kS}\kf(\kg(u,v),\kh(u,v)) |\frac{\partial (x,y)}{\partial (u,v)}|du\;dv.$
  • If $F$ is continuous on $\kR,$ then $$\begin{array}{rl}\iiint\limits_{\kR}\kF(x,y,z) dV & =\iiint\limits_{\kG}\kF(\kg(u,v,w),\kh(u,v,w),k(u,v,w)) |\frac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (u,v,w)}|du\;dv\;dw \\ & =\iiint\limits_{\kG}\kH(u,v,w) |\kJ(u,v,w)|du\;dv\;dw.\end{array}$$

exercises.prompt: Let a transformation $T$ be defined as $T(u,v)=(x,y)$ where $x=u+v,y=3v.$ Find the image of the rectangle $G=\{(u,v)\text{:}\;0\le u\le 1,0\le v\le 2\}$ from the $uv\text{-plane}$ after the transformation into a region $R$ in the $xy\text{-plane}\text{.}$ Show that $T$ is a one-to-one transformation and find $T^{-1}(x,y).$
Find the Jacobian of the transformation: $T(u,v)=(u+v,2v).$

answer.solution: $J(u,v)=\frac{\partial (x,y)}{\partial (u,v)}=|\begin{array}{lll}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{array}|=|\begin{array}{lll}1 & & 1 \\ 0 & & 2\end{array}|=2$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, determine whether the transformations $T:S\to R$ are one-to-one or not.

$T(u,v)=(2u-v,u),$ where $S$ is the triangle of vertices $(-1,1),(-1,-1),\text{and}\;(1,-1).$

answer.solution: $T$ is one-to-one: We argue by contradiction. $T(u_{1},v_{1})=T(u_{2},v_{2})$ implies $2u_{1}-v_{1}=2u_{2}-v_{2}$ and $u_{1}=u_{2}.$ Thus, $u_{1}=u_{2}$ and $v_{1}=v_{2}.$

a. Find a transformation $T:S\to R,$ $T(u,v)=(x,y)=(au+bv,cu+dv),$ where $a,b,c$ and $d$ are real numbers with $ad-bc\ne 0$ such that $T^{-1}(0,0)=(0,0),$ $T^{-1}(2,0)=(1,0),$ and $T^{-1}(1,3)=(0,1).$

Show that $\iint\limits_{R}f(\sqrt{\frac{x^{2}}{3}+\frac{y^{2}}{3}}) dA=2\pi \sqrt{15}\int_0^{1} f(\rho ) \rho \;d\rho ,$ where $f$ is a continuous function on $[0,1]$ and $R$ is the region bounded by the ellipse $5x^{2}+3y^{2}=15.$

answer.solution: Take $x=\sqrt{3}\,\rho\cos\theta,$ $y=\sqrt{5}\,\rho\sin\theta,$ which carries the rectangle $0\le\rho\le 1,$ $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$ onto the region inside the ellipse $5x^{2}+3y^{2}=15,$ that is $\frac{x^{2}}{3}+\frac{y^{2}}{5}\le 1.$ Its Jacobian is $\begin{vmatrix}\sqrt{3}\cos\theta & -\sqrt{3}\rho\sin\theta\\ \sqrt{5}\sin\theta & \sqrt{5}\rho\cos\theta\end{vmatrix}=\sqrt{15}\,\rho,$ and $\frac{x^{2}}{3}+\frac{y^{2}}{5}=\rho^{2},$ so $\iint_{R}f(\sqrt{\frac{x^{2}}{3}+\frac{y^{2}}{5}})\,dA=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}f(\rho)\sqrt{15}\,\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta=2\pi\sqrt{15}\int_{0}^{1}f(\rho)\rho\,d\rho.$

exercises.prompt: Show that $\iiint\limits_{R}f(\sqrt{16x^{2}+4y^{2}+z^{2}}) dV=\frac{\pi}{2}\int_0^{1} f(\rho ) {\rho }^{2}d\rho ,$ where $f$ is a continuous function on $[0,1]$ and $R$ is the region bounded by the ellipsoid $16x^{2}+4y^{2}+z^{2}=1.$

answer.solution: Take $x=\frac{1}{4}\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta,$ $y=\frac{1}{2}\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta,$ $z=\rho\cos\varphi,$ the spherical coordinates of the stretched variables $u=4x,$ $v=2y,$ $w=z.$ Then $16x^{2}+4y^{2}+z^{2}=\rho^{2},$ the ellipsoid is $0\le\rho\le 1,$ and the Jacobian is $\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\rho^{2}\sin\varphi=\frac{1}{8}\rho^{2}\sin\varphi.$ Hence $\iiint_{R}f(\sqrt{16x^{2}+4y^{2}+z^{2}})\,dV=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}f(\rho)\frac{1}{8}\rho^{2}\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta=\frac{1}{8}(2\pi)(2)\int_{0}^{1}f(\rho)\rho^{2}\,d\rho=\frac{\pi}{2}\int_{0}^{1}f(\rho)\rho^{2}\,d\rho.$

A transformation $T:{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\to {\mathbb{R}}^{2},T(u,v)=(x,y)$ of the form $x=au+bv,y=cu+dv,$ where $a,b,c,\text{and}\;d$ are real numbers, is called linear. Show that a linear transformation for which $ad-bc\ne 0$ maps parallelograms to parallelograms.

answer.solution: A parallelogram is the set of points $\mathbf{p}+s\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}$ with $0\le s,t\le 1,$ where $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are vectors along its sides that are not parallel. A linear transformation satisfies $T(\mathbf{p}+s\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b})=T(\mathbf{p})+sT(\mathbf{a})+tT(\mathbf{b}),$ so the image is the set of points $T(\mathbf{p})+sT(\mathbf{a})+tT(\mathbf{b})$ for the same $s$ and $t,$ a parallelogram with sides $T(\mathbf{a})$ and $T(\mathbf{b})$ provided these are not parallel. Since $ad-bc\ne 0,$ $T$ is one-to-one, and the cross product of $T(\mathbf{a})$ and $T(\mathbf{b})$ (with $\mathbf{k}$-components $0$) is $(ad-bc)$ times that of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ which is not zero, so $T(\mathbf{a})$ and $T(\mathbf{b})$ are not parallel.

exercises.prompt: The transformation $T_{\theta}:{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\to {\mathbb{R}}^{2},T_{\theta}(u,v)=(x,y),$ where $x=u\;\cos \theta -v\;\sin \theta ,$ $y=u\;\sin \theta +v\;\cos \theta ,$ is called a rotation of angle $\theta .$ Show that the inverse transformation of $T_{\theta}$ satisfies $T_{\theta}{}^{-1}=T_{-\theta},$ where $T_{-\theta}$ is the rotation of angle $-\theta .$

answer.solution: Apply $T_{-\theta}$ to the image $(x,y)=T_{\theta}(u,v)$: its first component is $x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta=(u\cos\theta-v\sin\theta)\cos\theta+(u\sin\theta+v\cos\theta)\sin\theta=u,$ and its second is $-x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta=-(u\cos\theta-v\sin\theta)\sin\theta+(u\sin\theta+v\cos\theta)\cos\theta=v,$ using $\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1.$ So $T_{-\theta}\circ T_{\theta}$ is the identity, and in the same way (with $-\theta$ for $\theta$) so is $T_{\theta}\circ T_{-\theta};$ hence $T_{\theta}^{-1}=T_{-\theta}.$

exercises.prompt: Use the transformation, $x=au,y=av,z=cw$ and spherical coordinates to show that the volume of a region bounded by the spheroid $\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{z^{2}}{c^{2}}=1$ is $\frac{4\pi a^{2}c}{3}.$

answer.solution: Under $x=au,$ $y=av,$ $z=cw$ the spheroid $\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{z^{2}}{c^{2}}\le 1$ is the image of the unit ball $u^{2}+v^{2}+w^{2}\le 1,$ and the Jacobian is the determinant of the diagonal matrix with entries $a,a,c,$ that is $a^{2}c.$ In spherical coordinates the unit ball has volume $\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}\rho^{2}\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta=\frac{4\pi}{3},$ so the spheroid’s volume is $\iiint dV=a^{2}c\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3}=\frac{4\pi a^{2}c}{3}.$
